questions.text: What is the company's name?
questions.why: Used in document titles and file names.

questions.text: Which country is the company registered in? Use the two-letter code, for example IE, GB or DE.
questions.why: Sets which rules and market conventions apply.

questions.text: What currency does the company report in? Use the three-letter code, for example EUR.
questions.why: Every amount is compared in this currency.

questions.text: Which accounting framework do the accounts follow?
questions.why: Decides whether hedge accounting and some covenant definitions matter.

questions.text: Which best describes your role?
questions.why: Helps set the output at the right level of detail.

options.label: Board or executive committee
options.value: Board of Directors or Executive Committee

questions.text: Roughly what is annual group turnover?
questions.why: Sets which controls and products are proportionate for the company's size.

questions.text: Roughly what is the balance sheet total?
questions.why: Part of the size test banks use to decide which products they can offer.

questions.text: Roughly how much equity (own funds) does the company have?
questions.why: The third part of the banks' size test.

questions.text: How many legal entities are in the group?
questions.why: More entities mean more bank accounts, intercompany flows and approvals.

questions.text: Which foreign currencies does the company buy or sell in? List the codes, for example USD, GBP.
questions.why: Defines the FX exposures the policy has to cover.

questions.text: Does the company bid for contracts in foreign currencies that it may not win?
questions.why: Uncertain exposures need different hedging rules from firm ones.

questions.text: Does the company have a material exposure to any commodity or energy price, such as a raw material it buys or a commodity it sells? List them, for example steel, aluminium, natural gas. Leave blank if none.
questions.why: Defines the commodity or energy exposures the policy has to cover.

questions.text: Do funds move between the group's entities — for example intercompany loans, cash pooling or cross-charges?
questions.why: Decides whether the intercompany funding and FX netting clauses apply.

questions.text: Does the company have bank loans, facilities or other borrowings?
questions.why: Decides whether interest-rate and funding sections apply.

questions.text: Is any of that debt at a floating rate?
questions.why: Floating-rate debt creates interest-rate risk the policy should address.

questions.text: Do the loans carry financial covenants, such as a leverage or interest-cover test?
questions.why: Covenant headroom limits how much risk the company can take.

questions.text: Is any of that debt secured against company assets, or backed by a guarantee from a group entity?
questions.why: Decides whether the security and guarantees clause applies.

questions.text: How many banks does the company hold accounts with?
questions.why: Shapes counterparty limits and payment controls.

questions.text: Does the company hold deposits or money-market funds beyond its operating accounts?
questions.why: Decides whether an investment section is needed.

questions.text: How easily can the company open accounts or hedge with highly rated international banks?
questions.why: A rating floor is pointless if those banks won't deal with the company.

questions.text: How many people work in finance?
questions.why: Separation of duties has to be realistic for the team's size.

questions.text: Is there someone whose main job is treasury?
questions.why: Changes who can own day-to-day hedging and cash decisions.

questions.text: Will the board approve the policy?
questions.why: Sets the approval and reporting lines in the policy.

questions.text: Who approves an outgoing payment today, and up to what amount can they authorise one on their own? For example, "Finance Manager, up to £10,000".
questions.why: Sets the approval limits the fraud checks compare payment amounts against.

questions.text: When a supplier says their bank details have changed, is the change verified by phoning a number already on file, rather than one given in the message that reported the change?
questions.why: A callback to a known number is what actually stops a bank-detail-change fraud; without it, a changed detail is only ever caught after the money has gone.

questions.text: Does releasing a payment always need a second, different person from the one who prepared it, rather than one person able to release it alone?
questions.why: Sets whether this run's sign-off is the only control in the chain, or sits alongside dual release in the banking channel.

questions.text: Roughly how large are the company's currency exposures as a share of turnover?
questions.why: Larger exposures mean currency moves hit profit harder.

questions.text: How many people are involved in managing currency and interest-rate risk?
questions.why: Complex strategies need more people to run safely.

questions.text: How accurate are the company's currency forecasts usually?
questions.why: Less accurate forecasts call for lower hedge ratios further out.

questions.text: How precisely can the company predict when payments will be made or received?
questions.why: Uncertain timing favours flexible hedging products.

options.label: Longer, or often rescheduled
options.value: 3 months or longer / regularly delays or rescheduling

questions.text: How far ahead can the company see its currency flows with reasonable confidence?
questions.why: Sets how far out hedging can sensibly go.

questions.text: Put these hedging priorities in order, most important first. Reply with the numbers in order.
questions.why: Weights the trade-offs the policy makes.

options.label: Not missing out when rates move in our favour
Getting a better rate than the forward
